captions: Let's answer a question we have been circling.
Why is the entropy the compression limit?
What is really going on underneath?
The answer is one of the most beautiful
ideas in the whole theory — the typical
set.
Imagine flipping a biased coin — eighty percent
heads — one hundred times in a row.

How many different sequences could you possibly
get?
Two,
raised to the hundredth power.
An astronomical number — far more than the
atoms in your body.
But here is the thing.
You will almost never see the vast majority
of them.
A run of a hundred straight tails is
technically possible,
but you would wait longer than the age
of the universe to witness it.
The sequences you actually get all look,
in a sense,
alike.
They have roughly eighty heads and twenty tails,
in some order.
These are called the typical sequences.
And there is a stunning fact about them.
The number of typical sequences is not two
to the hundred.
It is roughly two,
raised to the power of n times the
entropy — here,
about two to the seventy-second.
That is a vanishingly tiny fraction of all
the possibilities.
And yet — this is the magic —

those few typical sequences together hold
essentially all
of the probability.
Almost every sequence reality will ever hand you
lives inside that small set.
This is the asymptotic equipartition property,
and it delivers compression on a plate.
We do not need codes for all two-to-the-hundred
sequences.
We can simply ignore the atypical ones —
they practically never happen.
We just number the typical set.

And labelling two-to-the-n-times-H items takes
exactly n times
H bits.
There it is.
The entropy,
made concrete.

Shannon's compression limit is really a statement
about

which sequences the world actually bothers to
produce.
And this is why compression only truly pays
off over long messages.
For a single flip,
there is nothing to exploit.
But stretch to thousands of symbols,
and the typical set sharpens,
the atypical fades away,
and real files collapse toward their entropy —
reliably,
every time.
The law of large numbers,
quietly doing the work.
